transcript.text: Scarcity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
WATCH OUT
Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING BETWEEN SCARCE USES

A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
CHECK YOURSELF
A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?
READY?

transcript.text: Determinants of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DEMAND SHIFT

Horizontal axis: quantity of coffee in thousands. Vertical axis: price of coffee in dollars. Two parallel coffee demand curves. D1 lies to the right of D0; at price $10, quantity demanded rises from 50 thousand on D0 to 125 thousand on D1.

At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?
READY?

Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-42
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate private, public, and national saving in closed and open economies.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

With net taxes T, private saving is Y - T - C and public saving is T - G. National saving is their sum: S = Y - C - G. In a closed economy, S = I. In an open economy, S = I + NCO; because NX = NCO in the course model, S = I + NX. These are aggregate identities, not claims that each saver directly funds one investor.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Budget surplus means T - G is positive; a deficit makes public saving negative.
Adding private and public saving cancels T and gives Y - C - G.
Use S = I only for the closed-economy model.
In an open economy, saving can finance domestic investment or net capital outflow.
WATCH OUT
Do not reverse the public-saving sign. T - G is public saving; G - T is the budget deficit. Also state the closed-economy assumption before writing S = I.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FROM COMPONENTS TO OPEN-ECONOMY SAVING
KEY RELATIONSHIPS
Private saving = Y - T - C
Public saving = T - G
National saving = Y - C - G
Closed: S = I
Open: S = I + NCO; NX = NCO

Let Y = $1,200, T = $150, C = $760, and G = $260. Private saving is $290; public saving is -$110; national saving is $180. If domestic investment is $140, then NCO = S - I = $40. The accounting identity also gives NX = $40.
CHECK YOURSELF
Private saving is $220 and public saving is -$50. What is national saving?
READY?

transcript.text: Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to omit one or more welfare components. Revenue is tariff×imports; each side distortion is a triangle. Total DWL is $144.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING IMPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the avocado export-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and exports at Pw=$10?

Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-34
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Long-run industry supply depends on how industry expansion changes firms' input costs. The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets. The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms' cost curves.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged.
A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition.
Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.
Read only the relationships displayed and apply the competitive-firm sequence in the correct order.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse industry cost conditions. If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING LONG-RUN INDUSTRY SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: industry quantity; vertical axis: price. The single line labeled LRS slopes upward from about price 18 at quantity 0 to just above price 50 near quantity 105. There are no demand curves or marked equilibrium points. Values are approximate readings from the displayed scale.

The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward, rising from roughly $18 at very low output to above $50 near 105 units. Industry expansion therefore raises the long-run equilibrium price. That pattern is consistent with an increasing-cost industry in which entry bids up specialized inputs or other production costs.
CHECK YOURSELF
Graph analysis 13: What can produce the upward-sloping long-run industry supply shown?

Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-49
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume equilibrium is efficient. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NASH EQUILIBRIUM

For each strategy of the other player, mark the action that gives a player the larger payoff. In the displayed matrix, row A against column X gives (9, 9), while switching unilaterally to row B would lower the row player's payoff from 9 to 3. The column player also prefers X to Y when row A is chosen, so (A, X) is a cell of mutual best responses and is a Nash equilibrium.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why must payoff order be stated?

transcript.text: Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-52
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Tacit coordination occurs when firms align behavior without an explicit agreement, while nonprice competition uses quality, service, or advertising rather than price cuts. Advertising can shape demand in both markets. Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price. Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes.
A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical.
Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.
A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume price is irrelevant. Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions. A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RECOGNIZING NONPRICE COMPETITION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price and cost. Demand D has a kink at approximately quantity 20 and price 50: it is steeper to the left and flatter to the right. MR has two downward-sloping branches separated by a discontinuity at the kink quantity. MC is horizontal at approximately $36. The owner-reviewed worked example treats MC as lying within the MR gap to illustrate price rigidity. The graph geometry is retained as reviewed.

The kink in demand occurs near 20 units and a price of $50. Because the marginal-revenue curve has a gap at that output, modest changes in MC around $36 need not change the chosen price or quantity. The model explains price rigidity while reminding us that oligopolists can still compete through quality, service, and advertising.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does parallel pricing prove collusion?
READY?

Externalities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-54
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare private and social incentives and identify the efficient quantity.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on someone outside a transaction. Negative externalities make private decision makers ignore part of social cost; positive externalities make them ignore part of social benefit. Efficiency uses all marginal social costs and benefits.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Ask whether the spillover is a cost or benefit and whether it comes from production or consumption.
Negative: MSC > MPC or MPB > MSB, so the market quantity is too high.
Positive: MSB > MPB or MPC > MSC, so the market quantity is too low.
Corrective taxes, subsidies, permits, regulation, or bargaining can internalize the spillover.
WATCH OUT
Do not label every harmful outcome an externality. A spillover must affect a third party and be missing from the market price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NEGATIVE PRODUCTION EXTERNALITY

Negative production externality in fast-fashion garments. Horizontal axis: quantity of garments in millions, with labeled ticks from 40 to 320. Vertical axis: marginal benefit and cost, with labeled dollar ticks from 3 to 24. MPB slopes downward from 21 to 9; MPC slopes upward from 3 to 15; MSC slopes upward from 9 to 21, six dollars above MPC throughout. MPB and MPC intersect at 240 million garments and 12 dollars. MPB and MSC intersect at 160 million garments and 15 dollars. Dashed guides mark both quantities and values.

Fast-fashion production creates a $6 external cost per garment, so MSC lies $6 above MPC. The market produces 240 million garments where MPB = MPC at $12. Efficiency occurs at 160 million garments where MPB = MSC at $15, eliminating 80 million units of overproduction. A $6 corrective tax aligns private and social marginal cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
If MSB lies above MPB, is the unregulated market quantity too high or too low?
READY?

Public Goods & Common Resources
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-55
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Classify goods and apply efficient provision and resource-use rules.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Excludability asks whether nonpayers can be kept out; rivalry asks whether one person's use reduces another's. Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, common resources are nonexcludable and rival, club goods are excludable and nonrival, and private goods are excludable and rival.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Free riding can make private payments understate total social willingness to pay for a public good.
Vertically sum individual marginal benefits to obtain MSB for a shared quantity.
Provide the efficient public-good quantity where MSB = MC.
Common resources tend toward overuse; property rights, access rules, or practical exclusion can change incentives.
WATCH OUT
Do not classify a good by who supplies it. Government provision does not automatically make a good nonexcludable or nonrival.
WORKED EXAMPLE: VERTICAL SUMMATION

Horizontal axis: community fireworks displays per summer; vertical axis: marginal benefit / cost in thousands of dollars per display. Dashed North MB falls from 50 at zero displays to 30 at four; dashed South MB falls from 40 to 20 at four and reaches zero at eight. Solid MSB is their vertical sum: 90 at zero and 50 at four. Horizontal MC is 50. At four displays, guides mark North 30, South 20 and the MSB-MC intersection at 50. MSB then falls to zero at ten displays.

At four community fireworks displays, North's marginal benefit is $30,000 and South's is $20,000. Because both communities consume the same shared quantity, MSB is the vertical sum: $50,000. MC is also $50,000, so four displays are efficient. Summing quantities horizontally would be incorrect.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which combination describes a common resource: excludable/nonrival or nonexcludable/rival?

Consumer Choice
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-58
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows every bundle a consumer can afford at given income and prices. Its intercepts are income divided by each good's price, and its slope is the negative relative price. Preferences rank feasible bundles; the optimum is the highest attainable indifference curve, usually where MRS equals the price ratio.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
At an interior optimum, marginal utility per dollar is equal across goods.
WATCH OUT
Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BEST AFFORDABLE BUNDLE

Horizontal axis: Good X; vertical axis: Good Y. A straight budget line runs from 40 units of Y at X = 0 to 20 units of X at Y = 0. Marked bundle A is X = 10 and Y = 20. At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.
CHECK YOURSELF
If only the price of Y falls, does the budget line shift in parallel or pivot?
